DATA 550 Lab 3 - Communication visualizations¶

There are two versions of this lab, one in Python and one in R. The R lab will use ggplot and the Python lab will use Altair.

This is the Python version.

Each partner should choose a version to complete, though keep in mind that you are required to alternate between completing the R labs and the Python labs to get experience using both languages.

Acknowledgemnts¶

This lab was lightly adapted from the one created by Joel Ostblom for the DSCI 531 version of Data Viz I in the 2020/21 Academic year.

0. So we meet again...¶

I am sure you have heard, turns out Bestflix did not make it. Copyright issues they said, can you believe it?? I can't, there must have been more to this story... And the only other person with knowledge of this enterprise was... YOU!

In the spirit of a true comic book criminal, I will scale my revenge for this set back completely out of proportion and attempt world dominion. Don't worry, there will be no blood shed, I operate with class so my plan here is to brainwash people into thinking that I am actually good for them and then reap personal benefits once in power, creative isn't it?

To convince the pleb... I mean honorary citizens of the world to vote for me, I have made several key visualizations showing what an ideal candidate I am. The only way to stop me (hmm why am I telling you this again...) is to debunk these visualizations and show voters the errors of my ways (this is clearly a fictional scenario since we are assuming that each person acts rationally and is convinced by data).

Below is my publicly distributed campaign material covering these four main area:

  1. The current dramatic increase in job dissatisfaction
  2. My previous record on increasing job wages for all
  3. Guns to the people
  4. My great approval rating

For each figure that I have made, I have also included the underlying data (imagine what a wonderful world it would be if that actually happened in real life...). You can find these datasets in your lab repo). For each question in this lab, your team has the following three tasks:

  1. Decide if you think my plot and my claim is misleading or not, why you think so, and how you would improve it in your version of the same figure (unless you think mine is already good). In addition to what we are learning this week, you will need to draw on your knowledge from last week for when certain plots are suitable and which are common pitfalls to avoid.
  2. To earn the people's trust, you need to recreate my plot to show that you know what I did. This includes axis labels, legends, colors, titles, figure size, everything as close as possible to the images I have pasted for each question below.
  3. Create your own better version of the same figure. Make sure that your choices are motivated in writing in point 1.

1. Dramatic decline in job satisfaction¶

The data¶

The cities-job-satisfaction.csv dataset contains (fictional) data from different cities around the world. In this data it was measured which proportion of people reported that they were unsatisfied with their work situation this year compared to last year. Each data point is a different city, and the value indicates the proportion of dissatisfied workers.

My plot¶

Altair¶

My claim¶

You can clearly see in this plot that people are dramatically more dissatisfied at work this year compared to last year. I have used transparency for the dots to prevent overplotting/oversaturation, so this means that the entire dark area has an even amount of cities throughout. In other words, there are as many cities that increased from ~0% to ~40% dissatisfaction as there are cities that stayed around 0%. That's atrocious!

Question 1.1¶

rubric={reasoning:2,writing:1}

  • Explain which mistakes (if any) I have done in my plot and provide an interpretation of the data that is more correct than mine. Be brief and clear in your answer.
  • You might have some ideas just from looking at my plot, but you will likely need to do some investigation yourself to answer this question fully. You can reference your improved plot as needed.

Mistakes:

  • Haven't grouped by city (aggregated would be better since there's alot of data) and the year data is on both x and y axis instead of just the x-axis. Additionally, the data is still overplotted since each dot represents a city, and it is difficult to see which cities increased or decreased.

Interpretation:

  • Between last year and the current year, the majority of job dissatisfaction scores was within 0-60%.

Question 1.2¶

rubric={accuracy:2}

Python

Recreate the Altair version of the plot. Your plot should look as close as possible to mine in the image above.

In [3]:
import pandas as pd

job_data = pd.read_csv('cities-job-satisfaction.csv')

base = alt.Chart(job_data).mark_circle(opacity=0.4).encode(
        x=alt.X('last_year:Q'),
        y='this_year:Q'   
).properties(title=alt.TitleParams(
    text="Dramatic increase in dissatisfaction in work",
    subtitle="Can't get no job satisfaction")
)

base

2. I will keep raising wages for all¶

The data¶

The wages.csv dataset contains (fictional) data from different companies in the city where I have been the mayor for the last few years. Each datapoint represents the average salary at a company. All the major companies in this city were surveyed both before I was elected and after a few years of my governing. However, this is not paired data, some companies are different from "before" and "after", so you do not need to do a paired analysis.

My plots¶

Altair¶

My claim¶

As you can see, I have been able to produce a significant increase in the average salary for workers in my city. This high raise almost certainly entails that all (or almost all) workers are receiving a higher payment than what they were before I started to govern. But since I know you are going to ask me for more robust estimates, I have also provided the median increase (which is even more notable) and the number of workers in each group (so that you can see that the samples are balanced).

Question 2.1¶

rubric={reasoning:2,writing:1}

  • Explain which mistakes (if any) I have done in my plot and provide an interpretation of the data that is more correct than mine. Be brief and clear in your answer.
  • You might have some ideas just from looking at my plot, but you will likely need to do some investigation yourself to answer this question fully. You can reference your improved plot as needed.

The mean and median salary (dependent variable) is on the x-axis instead of the y. Additionally, having axis labels that are more clear would make the plot easier to interpret. The axis also doesn't start at 0 (mean and median plots) which makes the difference look magnified. The plot would also be easier to interpret with a legend. The dollar signs are not neccesary in the x-axis. An example of a better interpretation of the data is the mean salary was 20.5 at the start of the governance and increased to 24 after.

# mean salary plot
salary = pd.read_csv('wages.csv')

mean_salary = alt.Chart(salary).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X(
        'mean(salary)', 
        axis=alt.Axis(format='$'),
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=[16, 24])),
    y=alt.Y(
        'when:O',
        sort=['before', 'after']),
    color='when'
)

# Count plot
count_data = {
    'when': ['before', 'after'],
    'count': [61, 61]
}

data = pd.DataFrame(count_data)

count_plot = alt.Chart(data).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('count:Q',
           scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 65])),
    y=alt.Y('when:O'),
    color='when',
    text=alt.Text('count:Q')
)

text = count_plot.mark_text(
    align='center',
    baseline='bottom',
    dx=7
).encode(
    text='count:Q'
)

chart = count_plot + text

3. Guns to the people¶

The data¶

The guns-r-us.csv dataset contains yearly data for the number of murders by firearms in Florida.

My plots¶

Altair¶

My claim¶

As you can see, just after the gun law in Florida was enacted, deaths from firearms plummeted. I don't really think there is much else to discuss here.

Question 3.1¶

rubric={reasoning:2,writing:1}

  • Explain which mistakes (if any) I have done in my plot and provide an interpretation of the data that is more correct than mine. Be brief and clear in your answer.
  • You might have some ideas just from looking at my plot, but you will likely need to do some investigation yourself to answer this question fully. You can reference your improved plot as needed.

The x axis values decrease from bottom to top (which is the inverse of regular graphs that start at 0 and increases towards the top), so it makes it look like gun deaths decreased, when in reality, they increased after the gun law was enacted.

Question 3.2¶

rubric={accuracy:2}

Python

Recreate the Altair version of the plot. Your plot should look as close as possible to mine in the image above.

In [71]:
guns = pd.read_csv('guns-r-us.csv')

area = alt.Chart(guns).mark_area(
    color='red',
    opacity=1,
    line={'color': 'black'},
    point={'color': 'black', 'size': 50}
).encode(
    x=alt.X('Year:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[1990, 2016])),
    y=alt.Y('Firearm murders:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[900, 0])),
    y2=alt.value(0)
)

text = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'x': [2005], 'y': [200], 'text': ['Gun law enacted']})).mark_text(
    align='left',
    fontSize=14,
    color='white'
).encode(
    x='x:Q',
    y='y:Q',
    text='text:N'
)

gun_plot = area + text

gun_plot

Question 3.3¶

rubric={viz:2}

Python

Improve my Altair plot. Chose the best type of plot to accurately reveal what the data looks like. Design the plot to be an effective plot for communication purposes, this includes proper figure size, axis/figure titles, font sizes, colors, etc.

In [86]:
base = alt.Chart(guns).encode(
    x=alt.X('Year:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[1990, 2016]), title='Year'),
    y=alt.Y('Firearm murders:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 900]), title='Firearm Murders')
)

area = base.mark_area(
    color='red',
    line={'color': 'black'},
    point={'color': 'black', 'size': 50}
).encode(
    y2=alt.datum(0)
)

rule = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'year': [2000]})).mark_rule(
    color='gray',
    strokeDash=[2, 5],
    size=1
).encode(x='year:Q')

text = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'x': [2000], 'y': [850], 'text': ['Gun law enacted']})).mark_text(
    align='left',
    dx=5,
    fontSize=12
).encode(x='x:Q', y='y:Q', text='text:N')

gun_plot = (area + rule + text).properties(
    title='Florida Firearm Murders Before and After Gun Law Enactment',
    width=500,
    height=350
)

gun_plot

My approval ratings are astronomical¶

The data¶

The (fictional) state-comparison.csv dataset contains a sample of voters from my state and a neighboring state of similar socioeconomic standard. Voters in each state were asked to rate their approval of the state's mayor on a scale from 0 - 10,000.

My plots¶

Altair¶

My claim¶

My approval ratings are through the roof! I am clearly doing a better job than my colleague and competitor next doors. And as you can see we sampled enough people to get smooth curves, which means that this difference is both likely to be statistically significant and the magnitude is just too big to ignore. There seems to be a few bores on the lower end of the spectrum, but can't win them all I guess.

Question 4.1¶

rubric={reasoning:2,writing:1}

  • Explain which mistakes (if any) I have done in my plot and provide an interpretation of the data that is more correct than mine. Be brief and clear in your answer.
  • You might have some ideas just from looking at my plot, but you will likely need to do some investigation yourself to answer this question fully. You can reference your improved plot as needed.

Y-axis ranges are very small, which amplifies differences making their magnitude look greater than they actualy are. The distributions have a large overlap region, which indicates that their distributions are similar (no statistical significance). A better interpretation would be: These distributions are nearly identical, suggesting no meaningful difference between your state and neihboring states.

state = pd.read_csv('state-comparison.csv')

ocean_plot = alt.Chart(state).transform_density(
    density='the value',
    as_=['value_transformed', 'density'],
    groupby=['where']
).mark_area(
    opacity=0.5
).encode(
    x=alt.X('value_transformed:Q', title='the value'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q', 
            title='density'),
    color=alt.Color('where:N',
                    scale=alt.Scale(domain=['My state', 'Neighboring states'], range=['#7FB3D5', '#76D7C4']),
                    legend=alt.Legend(title=None, orient='top'))
)

ocean_plot
